study_design_identified: Primary qualitative study (focused ethnography from 2021-2023 combining semi-structured interviews with 24 informal street vendors and 6 public managers, field observations, and qualitative content analysis alongside municipal statutory/policy document triangulation)
why_tool_chosen: Section 2 explicitly states that the research adopted a qualitative approach using focused ethnography (2021-2023), purposive snowball sampling, semi-structured interviews with 24 street vendors and 6 public managers, and qualitative content analysis (Schreier, 2012), with no quantitative comparative or survey regression component. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, primary qualitative interview/ethnographic case studies map directly to the CASP Qualitative Checklist.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (8 Yes, 2 Can't tell, 0 No on Q1-Q9; valuable qualitative contribution in Q10)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly state the study objective to examine perspectives of public managers (duty bearers) and informal street vendors (rights holders) in Juiz de Fora regarding water and sanitation access in public spaces, grounded in the human rights principle of accountability, to uncover policy, legal, and institutional gaps.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Section 1 Introduction, final paragraph (PDF p. 2)

domain_ratings.justification: A qualitative methodology is well suited to exploring informal street vendors' lived experiences and coping strategies alongside public managers' subjective interpretations of legal mandates, institutional responsibilities, and cross-sectoral barriers.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors justify adopting a focused ethnography (2021-2023) combining field observations of downtown public facilities, municipal statutory/policy document analysis, and semi-structured interviews with both street vendors and municipal managers across relevant secretariats/utilities to compare policy discourse against street-level practice.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Methodological procedures (PDF pp. 2-3); Section 3.1 (PDF pp. 3-4)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: While purposive non-probabilistic snowball sampling guided by theoretical saturation and recruiting 6 managers across 4 key municipal entities (SEPUR, CESAMA, SESMAUR, SEDH) plus 24 central-area street vendors aligns broadly with the study's aims, the paper provides only a generic description of snowball recruitment without explaining how initial street-vendor seed contacts were chosen, the demographic or fixed-versus-itinerant composition of the 24 vendors, whether any approached individuals refused participation, or the identity of an unexplained interviewee code ('CH_3' on PDF p. 7).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Methodological procedures (PDF pp. 2-3); Section 3.3 (PDF p. 7)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: Data collection combined focused ethnographic field visits mapped in downtown Juiz de Fora (Fig. 1), direct photographic documentation of public and private facilities (Figs. 2-6), and semi-structured interviews with 24 vendors and 6 managers continued until theoretical saturation, with original Brazilian Portuguese statements translated by the authors. Although interview duration, interview guide prompts, and audio-recording logistics are not detailed in the main text, the multi-source qualitative approach clearly addressed the research question.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Methodological procedures (PDF pp. 2-3); Section 3.1, Figs. 1-6 (PDF pp. 3-5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors briefly note that the first author lived in Juiz de Fora for over 20 years while having had no prior contact with the studied street vendors (citing Velho, 1979 on familiarity and detachment). However, there is insufficient detail to determine whether the researchers critically examined power asymmetries with precarious informal workers, social desirability among municipal officials, or how researcher positionality shaped interview questions and interpretation.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: The study reports formal approval by the Ethics Committee of the Federal University of Minas Gerais (CAAE: 65026722.2.0000.5149) and anonymization of interviewees via alphanumeric codes, although field consent procedures with informal workers are not elaborated in detail.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Methodological procedures, final paragraph (PDF p. 3)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: Interviews were analyzed using Schreier's (2012) qualitative content analysis with group-specific codebooks (detailed in Supplementary Material 1) and two-stage coding by the coder to assess intra-coder stability via ReCal2, achieving >80% agreement and Krippendorff's alpha >0.8. Themes are well supported by verbatim-translated quotes from diverse participants and systematically triangulated against municipal legislation, sanitation plans, and field observations, notwithstanding reliance on a single coder and one unexplained quote label (CH_3).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Methodological procedures (PDF p. 3); Sections 3.2-3.3 (PDF pp. 4-8)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly organized by duty-bearer and rights-holder perspectives, synthesized in Table 1 across legal/policy, institutional, and sociopolitical exclusion dimensions, explicitly evaluated against human rights accountability criteria, and accompanied by a transparent discussion of contradictory interpretations and study limitations.
domain_ratings.where_found: Sections 3.1-3.3 (PDF pp. 3-8); Section 4 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 8-9)

domain_ratings.justification: Valuable empirical and policy contribution — The study illuminates how household-bound statutory definitions of universal sanitation in Brazil (Law No. 11.445/2007 and Juiz de Fora Law No. 14.290/2021) and municipal departmental fragmentation exclude public-space informal workers, forcing reliance on precarious informal arrangements ('sevirologia') or paid commercial toilets. The authors appropriately bound transferability from a single municipality and outline concrete cross-sectoral and participatory governance recommendations.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable qualitative contribution to urban WASH governance and human rights accountability literature (narrative assessment)
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 4 Summary of the findings, limitations, and final remarks (PDF pp. 8-9); Section 5 Policy recommendations (PDF p. 9)

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / Not applicable — Focused ethnography (2021-2023) using one-time semi-structured interviews rather than a longitudinal cohort; snowball recruitment refusals or incomplete interviews are not reported (PDF pp. 2-3).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable (qualitative design with no quantitative causal effect estimation). Contextually, the study situates public-space WASH gaps within municipal fiscal priorities, procurement bureaucracy, heritage visibility embargoes, and street-level stigma toward unhoused populations (PDF pp. 5-8).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Strong for qualitative legal-institutional analysis — Directly cites, quotes, and contrasts relevant international, federal, and municipal instruments, including UNGA Resolution 64/292 (2010), Federal Sanitation Law No. 11.445/2007, City Statute Law No. 10.257/2001, State-Owned Companies Law No. 13.303/2016, Juiz de Fora Municipal Sanitation Law No. 14.290/2021, the 2022 Municipal Water and Sanitation Plan (Decree No. 15.646/2022), Halfeld Park heritage decrees, and CESAMA's 2021 Bylaws, testing managers' claims against statutory text confining supply/sewage definitions to building connections (PDF pp. 1-2, 4-6, 9).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Low-to-moderate concern — Qualitative content analysis used structured group-specific codebooks (Supplementary Material 1) and two-wave intra-coder verification achieving >80% agreement and Krippendorff's alpha >0.8, triangulated with field observation of downtown facilities and statutory texts; however, coding relied on a single coder rather than independent double-coding, interview guides and audio-recording/transcription procedures are not detailed in the main text, quotes are free translations from Brazilian Portuguese, and one participant code (CH_3 on PDF p. 7) is unexplained in Section 2 (PDF pp. 2-3, 7).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate for qualitative access and lived-experience assessment — Combines direct field observation and mapping of central-city public toilets, private pay-per-use alternatives (~US$0.50), and drinking fountains (Figs. 1-6) with street vendors' reported daily access barriers and coping strategies ('sevirologia'); no quantitative utilization rates, microbiological water/hygiene testing, or clinical health outcomes were measured (PDF pp. 3-8).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Low concern — Presents convergent and divergent perspectives across municipal managers and street vendors (including vendors preferring paid clean facilities over unmaintained free chemical toilets and managers disagreeing over statutory scope and budget feasibility), summarizes limitations transparently, and points to codebooks and reliability procedures in Supplementary Material 1 (PDF pp. 3, 4-9).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern — Convenience selection of a single municipality (Juiz de Fora, where the first author lived for over 20 years) and non-probabilistic snowball sampling of 24 central-area street vendors (out of an estimated 459 informal workers) and 6 public managers across 4 agencies. Snowball referrals through interviewees' social networks risk over-representing connected fixed-spot vendors relative to isolated itinerant workers, vendor demographics and refusal rates are omitted, and formal merchants, legislators, and civil society actors were not interviewed (PDF pp. 2-3, 8).

overall_narrative_summary: This primary qualitative study (focused ethnography between 2021 and 2023 in downtown Juiz de Fora, Brazil, combining field observations, statutory/policy document analysis, and semi-structured interviews with 24 informal street vendors and 6 municipal managers) was appraised using the CASP Qualitative Checklist. Methodological quality raises moderate concern overall (8 'Yes', 2 'Can't tell', 0 'No' across Q1-Q9, plus strong substantive value in Q10). Strengths include clearly articulated human-rights accountability aims, effective triangulation of manager and vendor testimonies with primary municipal statutes/bylaws (Law No. 14.290/2021, 2022 Municipal Sanitation Plan, CESAMA Bylaws) and direct facility observations, formal ethics approval, and structured qualitative content analysis (Schreier, 2012) with documented two-wave intra-coder reliability (>80% agreement; Krippendorff's alpha >0.8). Main limitations are incomplete reporting of street-vendor recruitment details (seed selection, demographic/occupational composition, refusal rates, and an unexplained 'CH_3' participant code on PDF p. 7), reliance on social-network snowballing in a single convenience-selected city, single-coder analysis without independent inter-coder verification, and minimal critical reflexivity beyond noting the first author's residential familiarity and lack of prior contact with participants.
where_found_summary: Study aims and legal framing in Abstract and Section 1 (PDF pp. 1-2); site selection, focused ethnography, snowball sampling, ethics approval, and qualitative content analysis procedures in Section 2 (PDF pp. 2-3); field facility observations, statutory/bylaw triangulation, and interview findings in Sections 3.1-3.3 (PDF pp. 3-8); synthesis (Table 1), limitations, and policy recommendations in Sections 4-5 (PDF pp. 8-9).
